name: Commercial Banking
description: The bank's provision of financial products and services to business customers — from sole traders through to large corporates. Encompasses day-to-day transaction banking, debt finance, international trade enablement, balance sheet and liquidity management, and payment acceptance. This capability is the primary commercial revenue engine for the institution and the relationship anchor that cross-sells into capital markets, insurance, and advisory services.
mandate_source: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA 2000) — deposit-taking permission under Part IV
Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 — Edinburgh Reforms, revocation of retained EU law, updated PRA/FCA objectives
Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) UK — prudential capital requirements for commercial lending
Capital Requirements Directive (CRD V) UK — supervisory convergence, governance, remuneration
Basel 3.1 UK implementation (PRA CP16/22, PS17/23) — output floor, revised SA and IRB approaches, phased 2025-2030
Payment Services Regulations 2017 (PSR 2017, implementing PSD2) — payment accounts, access, complaints
Business Banking Resolution Service (BBRS) — disputes resolution for SME customers up to £10m turnover
FCA SME lending review (FS23/3, ongoing) — affordability, transparency, and fair value for business lending
UK DORA-equivalent (Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, Part 5 — operational resilience) — ICT risk, third-party concentration, incident reporting
Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 (ETDA) — legal recognition of electronic trade documents including bills of lading and bills of exchange
Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2023 — FCA oversight of systemic payment systems
FCA Business Plan 2024/25 — focus on consumer/SME duty, operational resilience, financial crime

table_stakes: Business current account with BACS, Faster Payments, and CHAPS access
Online and mobile banking portal with bulk payment upload
Overdraft and revolving credit facility for SMEs
Commercial mortgage and term loan origination
Trade finance instruments: letters of credit, documentary collections, guarantees
Foreign exchange spot and forward contracts
Merchant acquiring with card terminals and online gateway
Cash management: sweeping, pooling, notional pooling
Relationship manager coverage for mid-market and corporate segments
differentiators: Real-time treasury management with API connectivity to ERP systems (SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics)
Embedded working capital finance triggered by supply chain events (approved payables, invoice verification)
Proprietary credit models using non-financial data (Companies House filings, Open Banking transactional feeds, sector benchmarking) for faster SME lending decisions
Digital trade finance platform with end-to-end LC issuance, swift messaging automation, and document verification
Multi-currency virtual account structures for corporates with cross-border treasury operations
Proactive FX risk advisory with automated hedging recommendations based on exposure scanning
Carbon-linked lending products with sustainability-linked pricing adjustments
disruptors: OakNorth Bank — data-driven underwriting for growth SMEs (£1m–£50m), proprietary ACORN credit platform licensed to other banks
Allica Bank — SME-focused challenger with relationship model and rapid commercial mortgage decisioning, targeting £1m–£100m revenue businesses
iwoca — unsecured SME lending up to £500k, uses Open Banking data, 24-hour decisions, penetrating the underserved micro-business segment
Tide — SME current account neobank, 600k+ UK business customers, bundled services (invoicing, tax, credit via partnerships), limited balance sheet
Revolut Business — multi-currency accounts, embedded FX, growing into business lending through EU banking licence
Adyen — enterprise-grade acquiring and treasury platform, direct acquiring without ISO middlemen, transparent interchange-plus pricing eroding bank MDR margin
Stripe — developer-first acquiring with embedded finance stack, dominant in digital-native businesses, Treasury API encroaching on float management
Square/Block — SME merchant services with bundled POS hardware, same-day settlement, and business account (SumUp is UK equivalent challenger)
MarketFinance (now Kriya) — invoice finance and pay-later for B2B trade, embedded directly at buyer checkout, bypassing bank invoice discounting
Satago — automated credit control and invoice finance, API-first, integrated into accounting software (Xero, QuickBooks)
Kyriba — cloud treasury and risk management SaaS, used by 2,500+ corporates globally, directly competing with bank-provided treasury portals
Coface / Euler Hermes / Atradius — trade credit insurance now embedded in receivables finance products, reducing bank credit risk but also disintermediating relationship
unbundling: SME lending unbundled by iwoca, Kriya, Capify using Open Banking data — bank loses origination and holds none of the risk
Invoice finance unbundled by MarketFinance/Kriya and Satago — integrated directly into accounting software, removing bank from the receivables finance conversation
Merchant acquiring unbundled by Adyen, Stripe, Square — bank acquirer loses the merchant relationship; gateway, fraud, and treasury functions migrate to the processor
Foreign exchange unbundled by Ebury, Equals Money (formerly FairFX), and Caxton Business — mid-market corporates accessing ECN pricing without bank FX desk involvement
Trade finance document handling unbundled by specialist platforms — Bolero, essDOCS, and (until failure) Contour attempted to remove bank document-checking manual effort
Treasury management unbundled by Kyriba, FIS Integrity — corporates consolidate banking relationships through a TMS that talks to multiple banks via SWIFT or API, reducing single-bank stickiness
rebundling: Tide and Revolut Business rebundling current account + invoicing + lending + FX into a single SME platform, reducing the need for a traditional bank
Adyen rebundling acquiring + issuing + treasury (Adyen for Platforms) for marketplace businesses — single provider for money-in and money-out
OakNorth ACORN platform being white-labelled to other banks — rebundling the credit decisioning capability but not the customer relationship
Embedded finance platforms (Railsbank/Railsr, Griffin) enabling non-banks to offer business accounts natively within their SaaS product — bypassing bank distribution entirely
Supply chain finance platforms (Taulia, PrimeRevenue, C2FO) rebundling buyer-approved payables, dynamic discounting, and working capital into a single corporate portal
switching_drivers: Relationship quality: access to a senior RM with sector expertise and credit authority — the primary retention driver in mid-market and corporate segments
Digital onboarding speed: SME account opening measured in days vs weeks is now a differentiator — challengers open in 24 hours, incumbents often take 5-15 days
Lending speed and transparency: time-to-decision on term loans and overdrafts — challengers making credit decisions in hours vs weeks for incumbents
FX pricing transparency: ECN pricing from fintechs vs opaque spread pricing from bank desks — large mid-market FX volume is highly price-sensitive
API connectivity: ability to integrate banking data directly into ERP/accounting systems via Open Banking or proprietary APIs — treasurers increasingly demand this
Business bank account portability: FCA consultation on CASS for business accounts — switching friction is currently high and regulatorily in focus

Switching friction is high for corporates: multi-product relationships with embedded liquidity structures, covenant covenants, and credit facilities take 6-12 months to migrate — this structural stickiness is the Big 4's primary moat

current: Basel 3.1 UK — PRA PS17/23 finalised rules, phased implementation from 1 January 2025 to 1 January 2030. Output floor rises from 50% to 72.5%. IRB restrictions tightened. Revised standardised approach (SA) for credit risk increases risk weights on unrated corporate exposures. Direct capital impact on SME lending book and commercial real estate.

FCA SME lending review (FS23/3 and related CP) — ongoing review of whether the SME lending market delivers fair value and appropriate protection. Likely to result in new rules on affordability assessment, price transparency, and potentially extending Consumer Duty principles to business lending below a threshold.

FCA Business Current Account (BCA) switching — FCA monitoring of CASS business switching performance, considering whether to extend personal switching rules to SMEs. Business account portability reform is a 2025-2026 legislative candidate.

Payment Services Regulations 2017 (PSR 2017) — compliance framework for payment accounts including access to payment systems, safeguarding of funds, and complaints handling. Merchant acquiring subject to interchange regulation via Mastercard and Visa scheme rules.

UK DORA equivalent (FCA/PRA operational resilience policy statements PS21/3 and PS6/21) — important business services, impact tolerances, self-assessments, and scenario testing requirements. Third-party concentration risk in focus for trade finance and treasury technology providers.

Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 (ETDA) — in force September 2023. Gives electronic bills of lading, promissory notes, bills of exchange, and warehouse receipts the same legal status as paper. Foundational for digitising trade finance document handling in UK law.

UK MLETR (Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records) alignment — ETDA implements UNCITRAL MLETR principles in UK law. Enables legal recognition of digital equivalents of negotiable instruments used in international trade.
incoming_2_3_years: Basel 3.1 output floor — floor rises in annual increments: 55% (2025), 60% (2026), 65% (2027), 70% (2028), 72.5% (2030). Banks using internal models for large corporate exposures will see capital requirements increase materially. Estimated 3-7% increase in total RWAs for a typical UK commercial bank by full implementation.

FCA SME lending rules — expected final rules 2025/26 following consultation. Likely requirements: standardised APRC-equivalent disclosure for business term loans, affordability stress-testing requirements for facilities above £25k, cooling-off periods for unsolicited credit increases.

Business account portability / CASS reform — HM Treasury and FCA consultation expected 2025. Could mandate 7-day switching for business current accounts, reducing the switching friction that protects incumbents. Major strategic risk for Big 4.

Open Banking for business — FCA and PSR driving towards full API access for business accounts equivalent to personal accounts. Corporate API-first banking will become table stakes by 2026, removing a differentiator for early movers.

Stablecoin and digital settlement — FCA/Bank of England sandbox for digital securities settlement and wholesale CBDC pilots. Trade finance use cases (digital bills of lading settled in digital sterling) are the primary commercial banking application. 2-3 year horizon for production pilots.

FCA Consumer Duty extension signals — while Consumer Duty currently applies to retail and micro-business customers, regulatory trajectory is toward extending fair value and vulnerability requirements to broader SME segments. Banks should anticipate this extending to businesses below £1m turnover.

PRA third-party risk management — CP30/23 consultation on enhanced expectations for material third-party arrangements. Direct impact on banks outsourcing trade finance platforms (Finastra, Surecomp), treasury technology (Kyriba, FIS), and acquiring processing. Concentration risk reporting to PRA becomes mandatory.
enforcement_signals: FCA Dear CEO letter to commercial lending firms (2023) — focus on fair treatment of SME borrowers in financial difficulty, requiring robust forbearance processes and outcomes monitoring. Banks found to be applying inadequate forbearance face Section 166 reviews.

CMA Business Banking Market Investigation legacy — ongoing monitoring of undertakings including promontory bank referral obligations and BCA switching data publication. CMA scrutiny of challenger bank access to SME customers remains active.

FCA supervisory focus on operational resilience self-assessments (March 2025 deadline) — commercial banking payment services, trade finance platforms, and merchant acquiring systems are within scope as important business services. PRA has signalled firms are underestimating third-party dependency risks.

PSR market review into card acquiring (MR22/1.7) — published remedies 2023 including scheme fee transparency, directed enhanced reporting. Signals continued regulatory attention on merchant acquiring pricing and bank acquirer market power.

FCA review of non-bank lenders in SME market — shadow banking risk, concerns about under-regulated lending platforms using Open Banking data. Signals potential for regulatory arbitrage to close, levelling the playing field but also validating the fintech credit models.

PRA letter on concentration risk in financial market infrastructure — direct reference to correspondent banking, trade finance messaging (SWIFT), and the need for banks to map and stress-test critical third-party dependencies in commercial banking operations.

platform_options: Trade finance platforms — Finastra Trade Innovation (market leader, 40%+ market share), Surecomp RIVO and CLOZ, Wolters Kluwer (Euclid), CGI Trade360. These platforms handle LC issuance, documentary collections, guarantees, SWIFT messaging (MT700 series), compliance screening. The ETDA 2023 and MLETR alignment are driving vendors to build electronic document support.

Treasury management systems — Kyriba (cloud-native, 2,500+ corporate clients, API-first), FIS Quantum/Integrity (large corporate, complex derivatives), Finastra Kondor (trading book), ION Treasury (Reval, Wall Street Systems), SAP Treasury and Risk Management (embedded in SAP ERP estate). Banks offer their own TMS portals to corporates but compete against these SaaS products.

Commercial lending platforms — nCino (Salesforce-native commercial lending origination, used by Lloyds, NatWest, Santander UK), Mambu (cloud-native core banking API, used by OakNorth, N26), Finastra Fusion Loan IQ (syndicated and large corporate loans), Temenos Transact (core banking with commercial lending module). SME lending decisioning: OakNorth ACORN, Codat (financial data aggregation), Wiserfunding (SME credit scoring).

Merchant acquiring processing — Worldpay (FIS), Fiserv First Data, Global Payments, Adyen acquiring-as-a-service, Stripe Treasury. Banks can own the acquiring licence and merchant relationship while outsourcing processing to a service bureau. ISO model (independent sales organisations) is increasingly being bypassed by direct processor relationships.

FX and risk platforms — Finastra Kondor FX, FIS Quantum for FX, Murex (large corporate FX structuring), Bloomberg FXGO for price discovery and execution, ION's Openlink for commodity-linked FX. Mid-market FX platforms: Ebury, Corpay, Caxton (now Equals Money).

KYC and onboarding — Encompass, ComplyAdvantage, LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Refinitiv World-Check. Business identity verification: Companies House API, Creditsafe, Dun & Bradstreet. AML transaction monitoring: NICE Actimize, Quantexa, SAS AML.

Open Banking connectivity — Token.io, Yapily, TrueLayer (business API coverage is expanding but remains less complete than personal). For corporate API banking: SWIFT gpi, J.P. Morgan Onyx (institutional), Codat (accounting software API aggregation).
must_build_in_house: Credit risk decisioning logic and credit policy — the credit framework, covenant structures, sector exposure limits, and portfolio concentration rules are proprietary and commercially sensitive. Third-party models can inform but not own the credit decision.

Relationship management and client lifecycle — the RM workflow, client profiling, pipeline management, and deal origination are differentiators. CRM systems (Salesforce) can be bought but the process and data model must be owned.

Pricing engine for commercial lending — margin-over-base calculation, risk-adjusted pricing, fee structures, and profitability analysis at the deal level must reflect this bank's cost of funds, capital allocation, and hurdle rates.

Product configuration and commercial terms — facility structures, covenant packages, security perfection processes, and drawdown mechanics are institution-specific and require in-house legal and credit ownership.

Regulatory reporting — COREP, FINREP, PRA110, and Basel 3.1 RWA calculation require institution-specific data from internal credit models, IRB parameters, and legal entity structures. Cannot be fully outsourced.

Sanctions and financial crime controls — while screening tools can be bought, the policy, alert disposition, and escalation processes must be controlled in-house under PRA/FCA senior manager accountability (SMCR).

Customer data and relationship history — the full history of client interactions, credit events, and product usage is a strategic asset that must remain in the institution's control. Cannot be locked into a vendor's proprietary data model.
buy_candidates: Trade finance platform (Finastra Trade Innovation or Surecomp RIVO) — the SWIFT messaging, LC document workflow, and compliance screening in trade finance is highly standardised. Building in-house creates only compliance risk (falling behind SWIFT message standards). Buy is strongly preferred; the bank differentiates on relationship and credit, not document processing.

Treasury management portal for corporates (Kyriba or equivalent) — providing a white-labelled or integrated TMS to corporate clients is a buy-or-partner decision. Banks that build proprietary TMS portals face Kyriba's R&D scale advantage. Consider a partnership model where the bank's liquidity products integrate into Kyriba via API rather than competing with it.

Merchant acquiring processing (Worldpay/Fiserv bureau model) — the bank should retain the acquiring licence and merchant relationship but outsource card scheme connectivity, terminal management, and settlement processing to a tier-1 acquirer processor. This avoids the capital investment in payments infrastructure that Visa/Mastercard mandate.

SME credit scoring augmentation (Codat, Wiserfunding, OakNorth ACORN) — for sub-£1m SME lending, buying a data aggregation and scoring layer on top of Open Banking feeds accelerates decisioning without replacing the bank's credit framework.

KYC/AML screening (ComplyAdvantage, Encompass, LexisNexis) — sanctions lists, PEP databases, and adverse media screening are commodity inputs. Buy and integrate; do not maintain proprietary watchlists.

Commercial lending origination workflow (nCino) — the loan origination system, credit application workflow, and covenant monitoring can be bought on Salesforce-native nCino. This is the dominant choice among UK commercial banks. Differentiates on workflow configuration, not the platform itself.

FX execution and price discovery (Bloomberg FXGO or ECN integration) — for transactional FX below the bank's own liquidity, using an ECN or aggregator for price discovery reduces the cost of maintaining a full FX dealing operation in non-core currency pairs.

primary_revenue_streams: Net interest margin (NIM) on commercial lending — the spread between cost of funds (deposit rate + wholesale funding) and lending rate. Primary income driver for commercial mortgages, term loans, revolving credit facilities, and overdrafts. Basel 3.1 output floor increases capital consumption, compressing NIM on standardised exposures.

Trade finance fees — LC issuance fees (typically 0.1-0.5% of LC value), amendment fees, negotiation fees, documentary collection handling charges, and standby LC annual fees. High fee density relative to balance sheet usage.

FX spread on commercial transactions — the bank earns the bid-offer spread on spot and forward FX transactions. Commercial FX generates 15-40bps on notional for mid-market clients. Ebury and Corpay are compressing this for price-sensitive SMEs.

Cash management and transactional fees — account maintenance fees, payment processing fees (CHAPS, international wires), bulk payment fees, cash handling, and liquidity management fees. Repricing opportunity as rates rise (higher credit balances reduce fee sensitivity).

Merchant discount rate (MDR) — the percentage of transaction value retained by the acquirer, net of interchange paid to card issuers and scheme fees to Visa/Mastercard. Blended MDR for a typical UK SME merchant is 1.2-1.8% for card-present and 1.5-2.5% for card-not-present. PSR scrutiny on scheme fees is compressing total margin.

Lending arrangement and facility fees — upfront arrangement fees (typically 0.5-2% of facility value), annual commitment fees on undrawn revolvers (typically 0.25-0.5% pa), and early repayment charges on fixed-rate facilities.

Interest income on trade finance facilities — import and export finance facilities, invoice discounting, and supply chain finance carry an interest rate margin above base. Working capital finance margins are typically 2-5% over base for SMEs.

Derivative and hedging revenues — interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, FX options, and structured hedging products sold to commercial clients. Margin is embedded in the derivative pricing. Regulatory capital requirements (SA-CCR under Basel 3.1) impact the return on derivatives book.
margin_pressure: Basel 3.1 output floor rising to 72.5% by 2030 — increases RWAs for commercial lending, compressing risk-adjusted NIM especially for IRB banks with optimised internal models. Estimated 10-20% increase in capital requirement for some commercial real estate and unrated corporate exposures.

Challenger bank competition in SME lending — OakNorth, Allica, and iwoca originate at lower cost using data-driven models, forcing incumbents to compete on speed and price or accept adverse selection on credits too small or complex for challengers.

FX margin compression — Ebury, Corpay, and Equals Money offer transparent ECN pricing to mid-market corporates; bank FX desks face growing pressure to justify the spread premium through advisory and hedging value-add.

MDR compression in merchant acquiring — PSR MR22/1.7 remedies, Adyen and Stripe direct relationships, and the growth of Open Banking payment initiation (account-to-account payments) are all reducing the addressable MDR pool.

Rising funding costs and deposit competition — following Bank of England rate rises, business deposits attracted competitive pricing from challengers and money market funds, increasing the bank's cost of funds and narrowing NIM.

Operational costs of legacy trade finance systems — manual document checking, SWIFT message remediation, and paper-based LC processing keep the cost-to-income ratio in trade finance high. Fintechs operating on cloud-native stacks have a structural cost advantage.

Regulatory compliance cost — SMCR accountability, Consumer Duty extension signals, Basel 3.1 implementation, and DORA operational resilience requirements all increase the cost base without generating revenue.
cross_sell_hooks: Commercial lending to FX hedging — a term loan in GBP with USD revenue exposure is a natural entry point for an FX risk management conversation and structured hedge.

Business current account to merchant services — an SME with a transactional account is the highest-probability merchant acquiring prospect. Bundled pricing (account + acquiring) increases switching barriers.
Trade finance to working capital finance — a business importing on LC terms has a natural need for pre-shipment or post-shipment finance, and an import LC is the triggering event.

Merchant acquiring to business lending — payment turnover data from merchant services provides the most accurate real-time view of business cash flow, supporting faster credit decisioning and cross-sell of working capital facilities.
Treasury services to capital markets — a corporate treasury client managing interest rate risk via swaps is a natural prospect for the bank's debt capital markets and syndicated lending teams.

Business current account to cash management — as an SME grows into mid-market, the transactional relationship anchors a conversation about notional pooling, sweeping structures, and multi-entity cash management.

SME lending to insurance products — a business with a commercial mortgage or equipment finance facility has insurable risk (commercial property, key person, business interruption) that the bank can distribute through a tied or open-architecture insurance model.

sub_capabilities.name: Business Current Accounts
sub_capabilities.description: Provision and management of transactional accounts for business customers — sole traders, SMEs, and corporates. Includes account opening and KYB, payments (BACS, Faster Payments, CHAPS, international), direct debits, overdraft facilities, online and API banking access, and cash management services. The primary customer relationship anchor and cross-sell gateway.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Business current accounts are the foundational product of commercial banking — no specialist providers compete here in isolation. Tide, Revolut Business, and Monzo Business offer accounts but always in combination with other services; none focuses on transactional account infrastructure alone. The regulatory framework (Payment Services Regulations 2017, FSMA 2000 deposit-taking) is shared with other deposit products. Lifecycle phases (onboarding, day-to-day operations, closure) are entirely within the commercial banking parent domain. Scalability requirements follow the same demand drivers as commercial banking broadly. Strong RETAIN: this is the relationship anchor and the data source for cross-sell of every other sub-capability. FCA business account portability reform (2025/26 expected) does not change the sub-capability boundary — it changes switching friction, not the institutional responsibility.

sub_capabilities.name: Business Lending
sub_capabilities.description: Origination, underwriting, structuring, and lifecycle management of credit facilities for business customers. Includes overdrafts, revolving credit facilities, term loans, commercial mortgages, asset finance, and government-backed schemes (CBILS successors, Growth Guarantee Scheme). Covers both SME and mid-market corporate lending. The primary NIM-generating activity of the commercial bank.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Business lending meets three of four promotion criteria: (1) Distinct participants — credit committees, valuation surveyors, legal counsel, and guarantors are specific to lending and do not appear in account management; specialist lenders (OakNorth, Allica, iwoca, Hampshire Trust) operate in this sub-capability only. (2) Separate regulatory framework — consumer credit exemptions for business lending, PRA credit risk capital requirements under Basel 3.1, FCA SME lending review (FS23/3) creating a distinct regulatory perimeter, and the PRA's IRBA/SA credit risk regime. (3) Distinct lifecycle — credit application, underwriting, credit committee approval, legal documentation, drawdown, covenant monitoring, annual review, and workout are phases absent from account management. Independent scalability fails criterion (4) — SME lending demand broadly tracks the same economic cycle as account growth; no independent scaling event separates them. Decision: RETAIN but classified as close to promote. Rationale for retention: the lending lifecycle is deeply entwined with the relationship banking model — the RM who holds the account relationship leads the credit conversation. Separating into a standalone capability would fragment the relationship model without proportionate architectural benefit. However, the Domain Analyst should revisit this if the bank pursues a platformised SME lending strategy (e.g. using nCino as the origination system) — at that point the lifecycle independence would strengthen the case for promotion. The FCA SME lending review may also create a distinct regulatory perimeter that tips the test.

sub_capabilities.name: Trade Finance
sub_capabilities.description: Facilitation of domestic and international trade transactions through documentary instruments, guarantee products, and structured commodity finance. Includes letters of credit (import and export), documentary collections, standby LCs, trade guarantees, supply chain finance, invoice discounting, pre-export finance, and the emerging digital trade document ecosystem under the Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Trade Finance meets all four promotion criteria and is a clear promote. (1) Distinct participants — correspondent banks, shipping lines, freight forwarders, customs brokers, trade credit insurers (Euler Hermes, Atradius, Coface), SWIFT network operators, port authorities, and commodity inspection companies are participants entirely absent from all other commercial banking sub-capabilities. Specialist providers operating only in trade finance include Finastra Trade Innovation, Surecomp, Bolero, essDOCS, and (until its 2022 closure due to consortium governance failure) Contour. The ICC (International Chamber of Commerce), UCP 600, URDG 758, and ISP98 are institutional standards with no equivalents elsewhere in commercial banking. (2) Separate regulatory framework — ICC rules (UCP 600, URDG 758, ISP98), ISBP (International Standard Banking Practice), export controls and sanctions compliance (OFAC SDN, UK OFSI, EU Consolidated List) specific to commodity flows, customs law (UK Customs Duty, tariff codes, Rules of Origin post-Brexit), the Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 (ETDA) which creates a new category of legally recognised electronic transferable record, and UNCITRAL MLETR alignment. The compliance overlay for trade finance (dual-use goods, sanctions evasion typologies, proliferation financing) is materially different from standard AML/KYC frameworks. (3) Distinct lifecycle — trade finance has phases with no parallel in other sub-capabilities: instruction issuance, document presentation, document examination (5-day UCP 600 period), discrepancy management, reimbursement, and financing. An LC may be outstanding for 12-18 months through multiple presentation events. The end-to-end lifecycle maps to trade transaction flows, not the customer relationship lifecycle. (4) Independent scalability — demand for trade finance tracks international trade volumes (UK goods exports/imports), geopolitical risk events (which trigger surge demand for LC over open account), commodity price cycles, and Brexit-related trade friction, all of which are entirely independent of domestic lending demand. The ETDA 2023 is a technology step-change event that requires a distinct build programme. Market note: Contour (R3 blockchain-based trade finance network) closed in August 2022 following inability to achieve sufficient bank network adoption. The lesson is that network-effect platforms in trade finance are fragile — this reinforces the need for an in-house capability rather than full dependency on a consortium platform. What survived: SWIFT's Trade Services Utility (TSU), Bolero's eBL, and vendor-hosted platforms (Finastra, Surecomp). The ETDA 2023 now provides the legal foundation that Contour lacked at the common law level.

sub_capabilities.name: Treasury Services
sub_capabilities.description: Provision of cash management, liquidity management, and financial risk management products to corporate and institutional clients. Includes notional pooling, physical sweeping, multi-currency account structures, interest rate hedging (swaps, caps, collars), FX risk management, structured deposits, and the online/API treasury portal through which corporates access these services.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Treasury Services meets all four promotion criteria. (1) Distinct participants — corporate treasurers, CFOs with board-level derivative approval authority, Group Treasury functions, money market fund providers, swap counterparties under ISDA master agreements, external TMS providers (Kyriba, FIS Quantum, ION Treasury), custodians, and securities settlement agents are entirely absent from retail or SME commercial banking. The Association of Corporate Treasurers (ACT) and SWIFT define a separate institutional ecosystem. Kyriba serves 2,500+ corporates globally as a competing TMS portal — evidence of a standalone market. (2) Separate regulatory framework — interest rate swaps and FX options are regulated as MiFID II instruments (UK MiFIR retained law) requiring appropriateness assessments, best execution obligations, and trade reporting to the FCA. Derivative products require EMIR (UK EMIR) margin and reporting obligations separate from lending or payment regulation. Structured deposits may require additional disclosure under the Financial Promotion Order. These regulatory requirements are entirely separate from the PSR/deposit-taking framework governing accounts. (3) Distinct lifecycle — the treasury relationship lifecycle maps to financial year planning cycles (budget hedging), rate cycle events (fixing vs floating decisions), and balance sheet management horizons (5-10 year swap structures), none of which align with the account or lending lifecycle. Notional pooling structure implementation, ISDA negotiation (taking 3-6 months), and CSA (Credit Support Annex) maintenance are treasury-specific lifecycle phases. (4) Independent scalability — demand for treasury management products spikes with interest rate volatility (2022-2024 rate cycle produced record hedging demand), FX volatility events, and M&A activity, all of which are independent of SME account growth or lending volumes. Kyriba's growth demonstrates that a standalone treasury portal business is viable at scale. The DORA operational resilience requirements and PRA CP30/23 concentration risk expectations around TMS providers create a distinct technology risk management obligation.

sub_capabilities.name: Merchant Services
sub_capabilities.description: Provision of payment acceptance infrastructure to business customers. Includes card acquiring (Visa, Mastercard, Amex acceptance), point-of-sale terminal provision, online payment gateway, virtual terminal, and associated reporting, chargeback management, and settlement. The bank acts as the acquirer of record, authorising and settling card transactions on behalf of merchant customers.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Merchant Services meets all four promotion criteria and is a clear promote with strong market evidence. (1) Distinct participants — card schemes (Visa, Mastercard, Amex with their own rules and compliance regimes), acquirer processors (Worldpay/FIS, Fiserv/First Data, Global Payments), terminal manufacturers (Verifone, Ingenico, PAX Technology), Independent Software Vendors (ISVs) embedding payments, independent sales organisations (ISOs), and merchant risk assessors are entirely absent from all other commercial banking sub-capabilities. Adyen, Stripe, Square/Block, and SumUp operate as standalone businesses in this sub-capability with multi-billion dollar valuations — the clearest possible evidence of a standalone market. (2) Separate regulatory framework — merchant acquiring is governed by the Payment Services Regulations 2017, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard v4.0) with its own compliance and audit regime, Visa/Mastercard operating regulations and scheme rules (distinct from banking regulation), PSR MR22/1.7 (card acquiring market review remedies, published 2023), and FCA authorisation requirements for payment institutions separate from banking licence requirements. The PSR has direct oversight of Visa and Mastercard scheme rules, creating a distinct regulatory principal with different objectives from the PRA and FCA banking supervision teams. (3) Distinct lifecycle — the merchant acquiring relationship lifecycle has terminal deployment, PCI DSS compliance certification (annual), chargeback dispute cycles (up to 120-day retrieval window under scheme rules), and fraud monitoring thresholds entirely absent from the lending or account lifecycle. Settlement operates on a T+1 to T+3 cycle driven by card scheme settlement windows. Merchant underwriting assesses chargeback risk and sector risk (high-risk merchant categories) using a completely different risk framework from commercial lending. (4) Independent scalability — card transaction volume tracks consumer spending and e-commerce growth, not business lending demand or trade volumes. Black Friday, Christmas, and online retail growth events drive merchant services infrastructure peaks independently of all other commercial banking demand drivers. Card transaction growth is structurally driven by cash displacement — a multi-decade secular trend independent of the interest rate cycle. The PSR MR22/1.7 remedies requiring scheme fee transparency and directed enhanced reporting signal this sub-capability will have growing regulatory complexity as a standalone domain.

design_decisions.decision: Retain Business Lending as a sub-capability despite meeting three of four promotion criteria
design_decisions.rationale: Business Lending meets the threshold for promotion (3+ criteria) but the relationship banking model creates a structural argument for retention. The RM who holds the account relationship leads the credit conversation; separating the lending lifecycle into a standalone capability would fragment the client data model and create integration complexity without proportionate benefit. The lending lifecycle is tightly coupled to the account lifecycle at the point of drawdown (loan proceeds credited to the business current account) and repayment (direct debit from the same account). At this bank's current stage, retaining Business Lending keeps the customer's full financial picture in one bounded context. The Domain Analyst must revisit this decision if the bank pursues a standalone digital SME lending platform or if the FCA SME lending review creates a regulatory perimeter that operationally isolates lending from transactional banking.
alternatives_considered: Promote Business Lending to standalone capability — justified by distinct participants (credit committees, valuers, solicitors), distinct regulatory framework (Basel 3.1 credit risk, FCA FS23/3 SME lending), and distinct lifecycle (origination through workout). Separation would allow independent scaling of the lending origination platform (e.g. nCino) without affecting account infrastructure.

Promote with a shared Customer entity accessed via events — the lending capability publishes credit events (FacilityApproved, DrawdownCompleted) consumed by the account capability, maintaining decoupling while allowing the account to reflect facility usage.
design_decisions.rejected_because: The deployment consequence of promotion (separate database schema, separate application, separate test suite) introduces cross-capability join complexity for the most common journey in commercial banking: the RM reviewing a client's combined account and lending position. The promotion test threshold (3+) is met, but the lifecycle coupling at drawdown and repayment makes the boundary cut unnatural. Retain with the caveat that this decision is flagged for Domain Analyst review at Gate 1.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Trade Finance to standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: Trade Finance scores 4/4 on the promotion test and has unambiguous market evidence of standalone viability: Finastra Trade Innovation, Surecomp, Bolero, and the now-closed Contour all operated as standalone platforms. The Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 (ETDA) creates a distinct technology change programme (digital bills of lading, electronic promissory notes) that has no dependency on the account or lending capability build. The regulatory perimeter (UCP 600, URDG 758, ETDA, export controls, dual-use goods sanctions) is operationally distinct. The failure of Contour in 2022 is a design signal: the lesson is not that trade finance digitalisation failed, but that consortium-dependency is fragile. An in-house capability with API integration to surviving platforms (Bolero, SWIFT TSU) is the correct architecture.
alternatives_considered: Retain Trade Finance within Commercial Banking — acceptable for a bank with a small trade finance book where operational simplicity outweighs boundary clarity. The shared customer and credit exposure model would simplify the data architecture.

Outsource entirely to Finastra Trade Innovation as a managed service — reducing in-house build scope but creating PRA CP30/23 concentration risk and losing control of the customer relationship data in trade transactions.
design_decisions.rejected_because: The ETDA 2023 creates a mandatory build programme regardless of whether trade finance is retained or promoted. Given promotion is justified on all four criteria, the deployment consequence (own schema, own application) matches the natural boundary. Outsource was rejected because the trade finance client relationship and credit exposure data is too strategically sensitive to place in a vendor's proprietary data model.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Treasury Services to standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: Treasury Services scores 4/4 on the promotion test. The MiFID II/UK MiFIR regulatory perimeter for derivatives is operationally distinct from the PSR/deposit-taking framework — different booking systems, different reporting obligations (EMIR trade repository reporting), different counterparty management (ISDA, CSA). Kyriba's market position (2,500+ corporate TMS clients) demonstrates that the treasury portal is a standalone competitive arena. The bank's treasury services need a dedicated API layer for corporate ERP integration — this is architecturally cleanest as a standalone domain with its own event contracts.
alternatives_considered: Retain Treasury Services as a sub-capability of Commercial Banking — justified if the bank's treasury product range is limited to basic notional pooling and spot FX, where the complexity of a standalone deployment boundary is not warranted.
Integrate treasury services into a third-party TMS via API partnership (Kyriba white-label) rather than building in-house — reduces capital expenditure and competes with Kyriba's feature roadmap.
design_decisions.rejected_because: The ISDA/EMIR derivative reporting obligations and the MiFID II suitability and best-execution requirements cannot be delegated to a white-label TMS without retaining the bank as the regulated entity with in-house oversight. The Domain Analyst should determine the product depth (basic sweeping vs full derivative structuring) as this affects the scope of the Treasury Services capability build — the schema supports the full perimeter; the Domain Analyst may scope down for initial delivery.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Merchant Services to standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: Merchant Services scores 4/4 on the promotion test with the strongest market evidence of any sub-capability. Adyen (NYSE-listed, €18bn+ market cap), Stripe (private, $65bn+ valuation), and Square/Block operate as standalone businesses in this domain. PCI DSS v4.0 certification, Visa/Mastercard scheme compliance, and the PSR MR22/1.7 remedies create a compliance and regulatory programme entirely separate from the banking licence. Card transaction processing and settlement infrastructure (T+1 cycle) is operationally incompatible with the daily batch cycles of commercial lending or the T+2 FX settlement cycle.
alternatives_considered: Retain Merchant Services within Commercial Banking — workable for a bank with a small merchant acquiring book where the compliance overhead is managed by a single operations team. Reduces the number of deployable capabilities.

Exit merchant acquiring entirely and refer merchants to a third-party acquirer (Worldpay, Adyen) — removes PCI DSS compliance burden and infrastructure cost but loses the cross-sell anchor (merchant data is the best real-time business cashflow indicator for credit decisioning).
design_decisions.rejected_because: The strategic value of merchant data for credit cross-sell (real-time transaction volume as a lending signal) is the primary argument against exit. The PCI DSS compliance programme is substantial but not a reason for retention — it is itself an argument for promotion, as PCI DSS has its own annual audit, SAQ, and remediation cycle. The acquiring processing infrastructure buy decision (outsource to Worldpay/Fiserv bureau) is the correct cost control mechanism, not retention within the commercial banking boundary.

design_decisions.decision: Recommend buy for trade finance platform (Finastra Trade Innovation) and acquiring processing (Worldpay/Fiserv bureau), with in-house ownership of credit decisions, customer relationships, and regulatory accountability
design_decisions.rationale: The SWIFT messaging infrastructure (MT700 series), UCP 600 document examination workflow, and card scheme connectivity (Visa/Mastercard) are commoditised capabilities with dominant vendor platforms. Building in-house would require maintaining parity with SWIFT message standard updates, ICC rule revisions, and Visa/Mastercard operating regulation changes — a running cost with no competitive upside. In contrast, credit risk models, RM workflow, and pricing engines are proprietary and must be built in-house. The PRA SMCR accountability framework means a Senior Manager is personally accountable for credit decisions — this cannot be delegated to a vendor platform.
alternatives_considered: Full in-house build for trade finance platform — pursued by some Tier 1 banks (HSBC, Standard Chartered) who have the scale to justify it. Not appropriate for a UK commercial bank without a global trade finance book.
Full outsource of merchant acquiring including the acquiring licence — eliminates regulatory burden but loses the merchant relationship and the cashflow data that supports credit cross-sell.
design_decisions.rejected_because: Full in-house build for trade finance creates an unsustainable maintenance burden around SWIFT message standards and ICC rules. Full outsource of acquiring licence loses the strategic data asset. The hybrid model (buy the infrastructure, own the relationship and the data) is the correct architecture for a bank that is not at Tier 1 global scale.
